lesson.title: Research symposium: defend, review and close the evidence loop
lesson.short: Questions · peer review · limits · research synthesis
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: A good answer in discussion separates what the experiment establishes from what would require another experiment.
goals: Answer critical questions with evidence and calibrated uncertainty.
Give actionable peer feedback without inventing a grading scheme.
Identify the next experiment and preserve the final artifact.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
Study path. Bring the claim and limitations prepared in session 36. Match each response to evidence actually collected before rehearsing discussion.

This original companion follows the supplied syllabus; it is not an Edinburgh lecture or verified Canvas assignment. Activities and timings are practice guidance. Assigned readings, assessment rules, deadlines and submission arrangements remain unverified.

sections.title: Prepare for four kinds of questions
sections.html:
• Meaning: What exactly does the claim cover? Restate workload, metric and operating condition.
  • Fairness: Was the baseline tuned and given equivalent resources/quality targets? Point to the protocol.
  • Mechanism: Which ablation supports the explanation? Separate observation from causal interpretation.
  • Generality: What happens under different scale, skew, concurrency, data drift or hardware? State measured boundaries and propose a test for the rest.

Listen to the full question, answer the narrow point first, then add a relevant piece of evidence. If the question reveals a genuine flaw, acknowledge its specific effect on the claim. Do not improvise unrun measurements to keep the story intact.

Key takeaway

“We have not measured that” is a useful scientific answer when followed by the experiment that would resolve it.

sections.title: Worked discussion: three strong responses
sections.html:
Question: “Would two H100s double throughput?” If you measured only one device, answer: “We measured one device. Routing, data placement and merge/communication costs still need measurement; our result does not establish multi-GPU scaling.” If you measured both, give the actual ratio under matched workload and quality, along with those overheads. Do not infer 2× from device count.

Question: “Your median improves. What happens to the slowest queries?” First check whether you collected tails and failures. If yes: “Here is our p95/p99 and timeout breakdown; the claim is restricted where a subgroup regresses.” If no: “We measured the median but not tail behavior. That is a limitation; a timeout-aware tail measurement is the next test.” The median alone cannot supply either conclusion.

Question: “Does your LLM evaluator prove the output is correct?” Evaluator agreement alone supports: “It measures agreement with our evaluator; factual accuracy remains unverified.” If you also performed an independent held-out human check, state its actual guide, sample and result, then discuss the remaining evaluator-bias risk. The human-check sentence is available only when that evidence exists.

Exercise: a reviewer says the result is caused by giving your method more memory. What evidence resolves it?

Worked answer. An equal-total-memory comparison, plus a memory breakdown and a sensitivity curve, can separate algorithmic benefit from added capacity. If that experiment is missing, acknowledge the confound and limit the current conclusion.

sections.title: Peer review that helps another group improve
sections.html:
Suggested discussion form, not an official grading rubric. Record: the group’s central claim in your own words; the strongest supporting evidence; one unclear assumption; the most important alternative explanation; one concrete experiment or presentation change; and an interesting connection to another course topic.

Make feedback specific and proportionate. “The benchmark is bad” is less helpful than “The compared ANN operating points have different recall, so the QPS graph does not isolate speed at equal quality.” Distinguish a missing explanation from an actual methodological flaw. Avoid guessing about the group’s effort or intentions.

When reviewing theoretical work, ask for assumptions, statement, proof idea and counterexamples. When reviewing systems work, ask for correctness, resource boundaries, workload and comparison. Neither kind of contribution should be judged solely by a speedup chart.

Exercise: a group reports a negative result with careful controls. What useful feedback can you give?

Worked answer. Assess whether the tested hypothesis was meaningful, whether controls rule out implementation/measurement errors, and whether the operating boundary is explained. Suggest the smallest discriminating follow-up, rather than treating the absence of a positive speedup as failure.

sections.title: Synthesize the frontier themes with the core course
sections.html:
Learned cardinalities revisit selectivity, cost models and plan enumeration. Vector search revisits indexing, physical layout and approximation. LLM pipelines revisit relational operators and the cost of choosing equivalent or approximately equivalent plans. Disaggregation revisits buffer management, concurrency, logging and distributed coordination.

A shared research question runs through all four: What contract is preserved while cost is reduced? For an exact relational operator, the contract may be SQL result equivalence. For ANN, it includes a declared quality target and eligible set. For a semantic operator, it includes a defined reference/labeling policy. For recovery, it includes durability and permitted histories.

Write down the layer your project optimizes and the layer where benefit is claimed. Kernel speed does not automatically imply faster applications; improved average predictions do not automatically imply robust decisions; faster steady state does not automatically imply better availability.

sections.title: Close the project with an evidence handoff
sections.html:
After discussion, preserve the final code/configuration, data instructions, raw outputs, slides/report and a short errata or open-questions note. Record factual corrections from the symposium and update unsupported language in the report.

Choose one next experiment that would most change your belief. It might test a confound, extend to a new workload or characterize a failure. Explain why it is more informative than simply running a larger benchmark.

Follow the instructor’s actual submission and sharing instructions when available. This companion supplies no deadline, upload destination, marking weights or mandatory presentation format.

Exercise: discussion reveals that a figure mislabeled milliseconds as seconds. What should happen?

Worked answer. Correct the figure and any derived claims, preserve an explanation of the correction, and inform the relevant audience through the course’s actual process. Check source data and neighboring figures rather than assuming the error is isolated.

Key takeaway

Finish with a trustworthy answer and a reproducible path to the next question.

questions.question: How should peer feedback distinguish missing explanation from a methodological flaw?
options: Treat both as proof of bad intent.
Assign a grading weight invented by the reviewer.
Ignore all uncertainty.
Ask for clarification and identify the specific evidence or control that is missing.
questions.explanation: Actionable scientific feedback is specific and evidence-based; the official assessment scheme is separate.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What does improved median latency establish about p99?
options: Nothing by itself; tail behavior needs its own evidence.
Tail latency is irrelevant in every workload.
P99 is always the same as the maximum.
P99 must improve equally.
questions.explanation: A median summarizes the middle observation; it does not characterize rare slow requests or failures.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: A unit error is found in a final figure. What should the group do?
options: Correct it, check derived claims and communicate the correction through the appropriate course process.
Leave it unchanged because the talk is over.
Change only the title, regardless of data.
Delete the raw results.
questions.explanation: An evidence handoff includes factual corrections and preserves traceability. Unit errors can affect interpretation and derived claims.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What is the most informative next experiment after a symposium?
options: A test that could resolve the most important remaining confound or uncertainty.
A rerun selected only to produce a positive result.
The largest possible run regardless of question.
A different chart color.
questions.explanation: Choose the experiment by how much it could change the scientific conclusion, not merely by scale.
